result:
I have been thinking about how much we rely on small rituals to feel like ourselves. Not grand traditions, but the quiet, almost invisible things. The way I make coffee at 7:13 a.m., not 7:00, because the water needs to be hot enough but not impatient. The chipped blue mug that only I use. The three sips before I open my phone.

We tell ourselves these habits are trivial, but they are the scaffolding of identity. When they disappear, on trips or during illness, I feel untethered in a way I cannot quite name. I am not anxious, exactly. I am just less me.

Maybe that is why I love watching other people in public. The barista who always taps the espresso machine twice. The woman on the bus who folds her scarf the same way every morning. We are all performing these private liturgies in plain sight.

There is comfort in knowing that continuity is built from repetition, not from epiphanies. We do not become ourselves in one moment of clarity. We become ourselves by returning, day after day, to the same small, chosen actions until they feel like home.

If I lost everything tomorrow, I would want to keep the mug. Not for sentiment, but because some things should be allowed to stay constant while the rest changes. It is not the mug that matters. It is the proof that I can still recognize myself in the morning. And that is enough to start the day.
